cards.meaning: a friendly word when you meet someone
cards.note: You can say it at any time of day.

cards.meaning: a word when you leave someone
cards.note: 'Bye' is a short, friendly form.

cards.meaning: what people call you
cards.note: Ask: What's your name?

cards.meaning: a word that makes a request polite
cards.note: It often goes at the end.

cards.meaning: a word to start a question politely, or to say you feel bad about something
cards.note: 'Sorry?' with a rising voice also means 'Please say that again.'

cards.meaning: 1, 2, 3 and so on
the number 10
cards.note: Numbers one to ten: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten.

cards.meaning: money in the UK; one pound is £1
cards.note: One pound, two pounds.

cards.meaning: the hour on the clock
cards.note: Answer with 'It's ... o'clock.'

cards.meaning: the first day of the working week
cards.example: The office is open on Monday.
cards.note: Days start with a capital letter: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday.

cards.meaning: this day, now
the woman who is your parent
cards.note: 'Mum' is the everyday British word.

cards.meaning: a boy or man with the same parents as you
a person you like and know well
red, blue, green and so on
cards.note: British spelling: colour.

cards.meaning: the colour of blood or a tomato
cards.note: The colour goes before the thing: a red bag.

cards.meaning: what you drink when you are thirsty; also the sea and rivers
a hot brown drink
you carry things in it
you call people and send messages with it
cards.example: The phone is in the bag.

cards.meaning: a small metal thing that opens a door
cards.example: This is the key for the office.

cards.meaning: it takes people across water
cards.example: The boat is at eleven o'clock.

cards.meaning: hello, before midday
cards.note: 'Good night' is for leaving or going to bed, not for hello.

cards.meaning: a friendly question after hello
a usual answer to 'How are you?'
cards.example: I'm fine, thank you. And you?
cards.note: Add 'And you?' to ask back.

cards.meaning: what you say when you meet someone for the first time
cards.example: I'm Sam. Nice to meet you.
cards.note: Answer with 'Nice to meet you too.'

cards.meaning: goodbye, when you will meet again the next day
what you say when someone helps you or gives you something
cards.example: Here is your ticket. - Thank you.
cards.note: 'Thanks' is shorter and friendly.

cards.meaning: a question about someone's home country or town
cards.example: Where are you from? - I'm from Brazil.

cards.meaning: a question about the price
cards.example: A ticket, please. How much is it?

cards.meaning: a polite way to get someone's attention
cards.example: Excuse me. Where is the boat?
cards.note: Use it before a question to a stranger.

cards.text: Could you say that again, please?
cards.meaning: please repeat what you said
cards.example: Sorry, could you say that again, please?
cards.note: Asking someone to repeat is normal and polite.

cards.meaning: please speak more slowly
cards.example: Slowly, please. I'm new to English.

cards.meaning: the words are not clear to me
cards.example: Sorry, I don't understand. Slowly, please.

cards.meaning: a question about a word you do not know
cards.example: What does this mean? - It means 'milk from oats'.

cards.text: I stutter, so please give me a moment.
cards.meaning: tells the listener you may need a little time to say a word
cards.example: I stutter, so please give me a moment. A small coffee, please.
cards.note: A clear, calm sentence. You can say it at the start, or at any time.

cards.meaning: say who you are or how you are
cards.note: Always 'am' after 'I'.

cards.meaning: a question about the person you are talking to
cards.example: Are you a teacher? - No, I'm not.
cards.note: Put 'are' first to ask a question.

cards.meaning: say something about a thing, a price or the time
cards.example: It's ten pounds. It's eleven o'clock.

cards.meaning: say your name
say your country or town
cards.note: Countries start with a capital letter.

cards.meaning: name a thing or person near you (this) or far from you (that)
cards.example: This is my phone. That is a boat.

cards.meaning: say what is yours
cards.example: I have a bag and a phone.
cards.note: Use 'an' before a vowel sound: an apple.

cards.meaning: say you have more than one
cards.note: Add -s for more than one. A few words change: child, children.

cards.meaning: ask who a thing belongs to
cards.example: Is this your water? - Yes, it is. Thank you.

lessons.title: Hello and goodbye
lessons.why: A greeting opens every conversation, and a few ready-made phrases let you start calmly.

passage.title: Morning at the harbour
passage.text:
It is morning at the harbour. A small boat is here. Sam works at the harbour. Ana is new.

Sam: Good morning!
Ana: Hello! Good morning.
Sam: How are you?
Ana: I'm fine, thank you. And you?
Sam: I'm fine, thanks. I'm Sam.
Ana: Nice to meet you, Sam. I'm Ana.
Sam: Nice to meet you too, Ana. Welcome to the harbour.
Ana: Thank you.

Sam shows Ana the office, the cafe and the boats. At five o'clock, Ana goes home.

Ana: Goodbye, Sam. Thank you for today.
Sam: Goodbye, Ana. See you tomorrow.

drills.prompt: It is nine in the morning. You meet a person. What do you say?
drills.hint: Think about the time of day, and that you are arriving, not leaving.
drills.why: 'Good morning' is a hello before midday. 'Good night' and 'Goodbye' are for leaving.

drills.prompt: Someone asks you, 'How are you?' Which answer fits?
drills.hint: The question is about how you feel.
drills.why: 'I'm fine, thank you' answers 'How are you?'. The other answers are for different questions or for leaving.

drills.hint: You will meet again. When?
drills.why: 'See you tomorrow' is about meeting again in the future. Yesterday is in the past.

drills.hint: The other person said it first; you say it back.
drills.why: Add 'too' at the end when you give the same words back.

drills.hint: A small word is missing after 'I'.
drills.why: After 'I' we need 'am': I am fine, or I'm fine.

drills.hint: One small mark joins them.
drills.why: A greeting and your name can go in one sentence with a comma.

write.prompt: Write a short hello to a new person at the harbour: a greeting, your name and 'Nice to meet you.'

speak.prompt: Meet the Guide. Say good morning, say your name and ask how they are. Take all the time you need.

lessons.check: What do you say when you meet someone for the first time, and what do you say when you leave?

lessons.title: I am, you are, it is
lessons.why: With 'am', 'are' and 'is' you can say who you are, where you are from and what you do.
lessons.rule: Use 'am' with I, 'are' with you, and 'is' with it (and with one person or thing, like 'my name'). In speaking we often join them: I'm, you're, it's. To ask a question, put the verb first: Are you a nurse? Is it open?

passage.title: At the harbour office
passage.text:
Leo is at the harbour office. The Guide is there.

Guide: Hello. What's your name?
Leo: My name is Leo. I'm new here.
Guide: Welcome, Leo. Where are you from?
Leo: I'm from Brazil. And you?
Guide: I'm from Wales. Are you a teacher?
Leo: No, I'm not. I'm a nurse.
Guide: A nurse! That's great. You are very welcome here.
Leo: Thank you. Is the office open today?
Guide: Yes, it is. It's open every day.
Leo: It is small.
Guide: Yes, it is small, but it is warm. And the coffee is good!

drills.hint: Look at the first word.
drills.why: With I, always use 'am': I am, or I'm.

drills.hint: Which word goes with 'you'?
drills.why: With you, use 'are': you are, or you're.

drills.hint: Think about 'it'.
drills.why: With it, use 'is': it is, or it's.

drills.hint: The verb goes first, and it must match 'you'.
drills.why: 'You' always takes 'are', in questions too: Are you ...?

drills.hint: Start with the question word.
drills.why: The question word comes first, then 'are', then 'you'. 'From' goes at the end.

drills.hint: How many names are there?
drills.why: 'My name' is one thing, like 'it', so it takes 'is'.

answers: I'm Leo and I'm from Brazil.
I'm Leo, and I'm from Brazil.
I am Leo and I am from Brazil.
I'm Leo and I am from Brazil.
drills.hint: One short word can join two facts.
drills.why: 'And' joins two facts about you into one sentence.

write.prompt: Write three short sentences about you: your name, where you are from and what you do.

speak.prompt: Tell the Guide your name, where you are from and what you do. Then ask the Guide one question that starts with 'Are you ...?'. There is no hurry.

lessons.check: Which word goes with 'I', which goes with 'you', and which goes with 'it'?

lessons.title: Numbers, prices and times
lessons.why: Catching a number when you hear it helps you pay the right price and be on time.

passage.title: At the ticket office
passage.text:
Today is Saturday. Mia is at the ticket office at the harbour.

Mia: Excuse me. A ticket to the island, please. How much is it?
Man: It's ten pounds.
Mia: Ten pounds. OK. What time is the boat?
Man: The boat is at eleven o'clock.
Mia: Sorry, eleven or seven?
Man: Eleven. One, one. Eleven o'clock.
Mia: Thank you. Is there a boat on Monday?
Man: Yes. On Monday the boat is at nine o'clock.
Mia: Great. Thank you.

Mia has her ticket. The ticket number is fourteen. Then she buys a coffee. The coffee is two pounds. Now it is ten o'clock. The boat is at eleven. She has one hour, so she sits in the sun and waits.

drills.prompt: In the story, how much is the ticket?
drills.hint: Look at the man's first answer.
drills.why: The man says 'It's ten pounds.' Two pounds is the price of the coffee.

drills.prompt: In the story, what time is the boat today?
drills.hint: Mia checks this number. What does the man say back?
drills.why: The man says 'Eleven. One, one.' Seven was only Mia's check, and nine o'clock is the boat on Monday.

drills.prompt: Mia says, 'Sorry, eleven or seven?' Why?
options: She wants to check the number.
drills.hint: Eleven and seven sound a little the same.
drills.why: Saying a number back to check it is a smart, normal thing to do. It is not rude.

drills.hint: This question is about a price.
drills.why: Ask about a price with 'How much ...?'

drills.sentence: The boat is at nine o'clock ___ Monday.
drills.hint: Which small word goes before a day?
drills.why: We say 'on' with days: on Monday, on Saturday. 'At' is for clock times: at nine o'clock.

drills.hint: Start with the two words that ask about the clock.
drills.why: 'What time' comes first, then 'is', then the thing you ask about.

drills.hint: Is it one pound or more than one?
drills.why: More than one pound needs -s: one pound, two pounds.

write.prompt: Write the price of two things you buy often, like a coffee or a bus ticket. Use 'It's ... pounds' or your own money.

speak.prompt: Ask the shopkeeper the price of a coffee and the price of a ticket. Say each number back to check it.

lessons.check: How do you ask for a price, and how can you check a number you are not sure you heard?

lessons.title: This and that, a and the
lessons.why: Naming the things around you is one of the first and most useful things you can do in a new language.
lessons.rule: Use 'this' for a thing near you and 'that' for a thing far from you. Use 'a' when you talk about one thing for the first time: I have a bag. Use 'the' when you both know which thing: The bag is blue. Say 'an', not 'a', before a vowel sound: an apple.

passage.title: What is this?
passage.text:
Tom and Lena are on a boat. The boat goes to the harbour.

Lena: Tom, what is this?
Tom: This is a key. It is the key for the harbour office.
Lena: And what is that, over there?
Tom: That is a boat. The boat is red.
Lena: A red boat! It's nice. What colour is your bag?
Tom: My bag is blue. I have a bag and a phone. The phone is in the bag.
Lena: I have a phone too. This is my phone. It is black.
Tom: That is a good phone!
Lena: Thank you. Look, that is the harbour. We are here!

drills.prompt: The key is in your hand, very near you. Which sentence is best?
drills.hint: Near you or far from you?
drills.why: 'This' is for a thing near you. 'That' is for a thing far away. With one thing, use 'is'.

drills.prompt: A boat is far away, over the water. Which sentence is best?
drills.hint: Think about the distance, and remember the small word before 'boat'.
drills.why: 'That' is for a thing far from you, and one boat needs 'a': That is a boat.

drills.hint: 'Over there' tells you it is not near.
drills.why: 'That' goes with things over there. 'These' is for more than one thing near you.

drills.sentence: I have a bag. ___ bag is blue.
drills.hint: We already know which bag.
drills.why: The first time, say 'a bag'. After that we both know which bag, so say 'the bag'.

drills.hint: One small word is missing before 'phone'.
drills.why: Before one thing, say 'a': a phone, a key, a bag.

drills.hint: Start with the two words that ask about colour.
drills.why: 'What colour' comes first, then 'is', then the thing: your bag.

answers: I have a key and it is small.
I have a key, and it is small.
I have a key and it's small.
drills.hint: You do not need to say 'key' two times.
drills.why: You can put the describing word before the thing (a small key), or use 'it' for a thing we already know.

write.prompt: Look around you. Write two sentences: one with 'This is a ...' and one with 'That is a ...'. Add a colour if you can.

speak.prompt: Look at three things around you, some near and some far. Name each one out loud: 'This is a ...' or 'That is a ...', and say its colour. Go at your own pace.

lessons.check: When do you say 'this' and when do you say 'that'? When do you say 'a' and when do you say 'the'?

lessons.title: My family, your friends
lessons.why: Talking about the people in your life is how new friendships start.
lessons.rule: For more than one, add -s: one friend, two friends. A few words change: one child, two children; one man, two men. Say 'my' for things and people that belong to you, and 'your' for the person you are talking to.

passage.title: A photo on the phone
passage.text:
Ana and Sam are at the harbour cafe. Ana shows Sam a photo on her phone.

Ana: This is my family. This is my mother. She is a teacher.
Sam: And who is that?
Ana: That is my brother, Marco. I have two brothers. My other brother is at work.
Sam: Your mother looks very happy.
Ana: She is! And these are my friends from home. I have three good friends there.
Sam: Nice. I have one brother and two sisters.
Ana: Is this your water?
Sam: Yes, it is. Thank you.
Ana: Is your family here?
Sam: No. My family is in Ghana. I call my mother every Sunday.

drills.hint: Two is more than one.
drills.why: For more than one, add -s: one brother, two brothers.

drills.prompt: Which is right for more than one child?
drills.hint: This is one of the few words that change.
drills.why: 'Child' does not take -s. One child, two children.

drills.hint: How many friends?
drills.why: Three is more than one, so add -s: three friends.

drills.hint: You are asking who the phone belongs to.
drills.why: 'Your' means 'belongs to you'. 'You' is the person, and 'you're' means 'you are'.

drills.prompt: Ana talks about her own mother. What does she say?
drills.hint: The mother belongs to Ana, the speaker.
drills.why: Use 'my' for your own family, and put it before the word: my mother.

drills.hint: It is a question, so the verb comes first.
drills.why: In a question, 'is' comes before 'this': Is this your ...?

answers: This is my brother and this is my friend.
This is my brother, and this is my friend.
drills.hint: One short word joins the two sentences.
drills.why: 'And' joins two sentences about people into one.

write.prompt: Write about the people in your life: who they are and how many. Use 'my' and one plural, like 'two friends'.

speak.prompt: Tell your neighbour about your family or friends: 'This is my ...', 'I have two ...'. Then ask your neighbour one question with 'your'.

lessons.check: How do you say more than one friend? When do you say 'my', and when do you say 'your'?

lessons.title: Could you say that again?
lessons.why: Asking someone to repeat, to slow down or to wait keeps a conversation going; confident speakers do it all the time.

passage.title: At the cafe by the water
passage.text:
Omar is at a cafe at the harbour. The waiter is busy and speaks very fast.

Omar: Excuse me.
Waiter: Morning what can I get you?
Omar: Sorry, could you say that again, please?
Waiter: Of course. What can I get you?
Omar: A coffee, please.
Waiter: Small medium or large?
Omar: Slowly, please.
Waiter: Small... medium... or large?
Omar: Small, please. And what does this mean? Oat milk?
Waiter: It is milk from oats. It is very good.
Omar: I stutter, so please give me a moment.
Waiter: No problem. Take your time.
Omar: Thank you. A small coffee with oat milk, please.
Waiter: That's three pounds, please.

Omar pays. He has his coffee. He asks, the waiter helps, and it is a good morning.

drills.prompt: You did not hear the price. What can you say?
options: Could you say that again, please?
drills.hint: You want to hear it one more time.
drills.why: 'Could you say that again, please?' asks the person to repeat. It is polite and normal.

drills.prompt: The person speaks very fast. What can you say?
drills.hint: What do you want the person to change?
drills.why: 'Slowly, please' asks the person to speak more slowly. Two words are enough.

drills.prompt: You need a moment to say your next word. Which sentence tells the listener clearly?
options: I stutter, so please give me a moment.
drills.hint: You want the listener to wait for you.
drills.why: This sentence tells the listener what you need. Most people are happy to wait.

drills.hint: After 'I don't', use the simple form of the word.
drills.why: After 'I don't', the verb has no ending: I don't understand.

drills.answer: Could you say that again, please?
drills.hint: Start with the polite question word 'Could'.
drills.why: Polite requests often start 'Could you ...?' and end with 'please'.

drills.answer: I stutter, so please give me a moment.
drills.hint: First say what happens, then say what you need.
drills.why: 'So' links the fact (I stutter) to the request (please give me a moment).

drills.hint: A question like this needs a helping word after 'What'.
drills.why: Ask about a word with 'What does ... mean?'. 'Does' comes before the thing, and 'mean' goes at the end.

write.prompt: Write two sentences you can use when you need help in a conversation.

speak.prompt: Order a coffee from the shopkeeper. Ask them once to say something again, and once to speak slowly. If you like, tell them you stutter. There is no hurry.

lessons.check: What can you say when you do not understand, when someone speaks too fast, or when you need a moment?

placement.prompt: Someone speaks too fast for you. What can you say?
